chain.g: not having the earth as the center of an orbit

ety.text: Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros)der. Medieval Latin eccentricusder. Middle French excentriquebor. English eccentric From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.

senses.d: Not at or in the centre; away from the centre.

ex: As of 2008, Margaret had the most eccentric orbit of any moon in the solar system, though Nereid's mean eccentricity is greater.

senses.d: Having a different center; not concentric.
Of a person, deviating from the norm; behaving unexpectedly or differently; unconventional and slightly strange.

Of a motion, against or in the opposite direction of contraction of a muscle (such as results from flexion of the lower arm (bending of the elbow joint) by an external force while contracting the triceps and other elbow extensor muscles to control that movement; opening of the jaw while flexing the masseter).
Having or being an oospore with a single large oil globule on one side that displaces much of the ooplasm and forces the ooplasts to one side.
One who does not behave like others.
ex: Eccentrics live longer, happier, and healthier lives than conformist normal citizens, according to the neuropsychologist David Weeks.

senses.d: A kook; a person of bizarre habits or beliefs.
A circle not having the same centre as another.
A disk or wheel with its axis off centre, giving a reciprocating motion.
An exercise that goes against or in the opposite direction of contraction of a muscle.
ex: Research tells us that eccentrics, heavy partials, and static exercise may require several days or weeks of recovery time.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricus, from ex- (“away”) + centrum (“the centre”) + -icus. By surface analysis, ex- + centre + -ique.
